summary: Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1): solve one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 10 by MODELLING the situation with objects or drawings, then reading the answer off the model. The core skill is representing what the story describes (things arriving, leaving, two groups combined, two groups compared, or a mystery start), not keyword-matching. Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position; keep totals within 10 so counting stays manageable.
misconceptions: Keyword-matching ('altogether'→add, 'left'→subtract) instead of modelling the situation, which fails on compare and change/start-unknown problems.
Modelling only result-unknown structures and being stuck when the unknown is the change or the start.
Grabbing the two numbers in the problem and combining them regardless of what the story describes.
Miscounting the objects when acting out, or not matching the drawing to the actual quantities in the story.
For compare problems, adding the two amounts instead of finding the difference.

activities.title: Story-modelling with counters and a mat
steps: Listen to or look at a short situation, e.g. 'There are 6 apples on the tree; the wind blows 2 down.'
Take 6 apple counters and place them on a mat to match the start of the story.
Act out what happens — move the 2 fallen apples to the ground, or cross them out on a drawing.
Count what is left on the tree and say the answer aloud (4).
Retell the story in your own words and point to each quantity (the 6, the 2, what's left) in your model.
Repeat with a joining story, e.g. 'Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now?', adding counters to match and reading off the total (7).
activities.insight: You don't need a rule to decide 'add' or 'subtract' — you build what actually happened in the story with objects, and the answer is simply what you can then see and count.

activities.title: Part-whole and compare: beyond result-unknown
steps: Model a put-together problem with a missing part, e.g. 'There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?'
Build the whole (7) and lay out the known part (4) using a part-part-whole frame.
Find the gap — the blue counters needed to fill the whole — and count them to give the answer (3).
Model a simple compare problem, e.g. 'how many more', by lining up two groups side by side (a bar/tape layout) and finding the difference.
For each problem, say whether it is a putting-together story or a comparing story, and explain how your drawing matches the words.
activities.insight: When the unknown is a part or a difference, you still build the situation — lay out what you know and find what's missing — rather than just combining the two numbers you can see.

activities.title: Narrate and show (talk alongside the model)
steps: Tell an adult or peer what is happening in the story in your own words.
As you narrate, show each step on the objects or drawing ('first there were six… then two fell…').
Answer prompts such as 'which part do you already know?' and 'what are we trying to find?' while pointing to the model.
activities.insight: Putting the story into your own words and linking each phrase to a quantity in your model builds sense-making, so the words guide the action rather than triggering a reflex operation.

checkQuestion: Use the counters to solve these. (1) There are 6 apples and 2 are eaten — how many are left? (2) Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now? (3) There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?
checkAnswer: (1) 4; (2) 7; (3) 3 — with the situation modelled on the counters (take-away, join, and part-unknown respectively).
